slides.title: Productivity Measures: Average Product
slides.text:
Productivity Measures: Average Product
Average Product of an Input: Measure of output produced per unit of input.
Average Product of Labor: APL = Q/L.
Measures the output of an “average” worker.
Example: Q = F(K,L) = K.5 L.5
If the inputs are K = 16 and L = 16, then the average product of labor is APL = [(16) 0.5(16)0.5]/16 = 1.
Average Product of Capital: APK = Q/K.
Measures the output of an “average” unit of capital.
Example: Q = F(K,L) = K.5 L.5
If the inputs are K = 16 and L = 16, then the average product of capital is APK = [(16)0.5(16)0.5]/16 = 1.

slides.title: Productivity Measures: Marginal Product
slides.text:
Productivity Measures: Marginal Product
Marginal Product: Change in total output attributable to the last unit of an input.
Marginal Product of Labor: MPL = Q/L
Measures the output produced by the last worker.
Slope of the short-run production function (with respect to labor).
Marginal Product of Capital: MPK = Q/K
Measures the output produced by the last unit of capital.
When capital is allowed to vary in the short run, MPK is the slope of the production function (with respect to capital).

slides.title: Law of Variable Proportions
slides.text:
Law of Variable Proportions
Short run: Law of Variable Proportions ⇒ Variation in Marginal product of labour (MPL)
Law of Variable Proportions: As successive units of a variable input are added to a fixed input, the marginal product of the variable input first increases, reaches a maximum, and eventually decreases.
Initially, the fixed input is underutilised. Adding variable inputs allows: Specialisation (workers can divide tasks), better coordination (workers can assist each other) and better utilisation of the fixed input (machines/factory space are used more effectively).
So each additional worker can contribute more than the previous worker.
Eventually, the fixed input becomes a constraint. Too many variable inputs sharing the same machines means workers have to wait for machines, the space becomes crowded and opportunities for further specialisation are already exhausted.
Therefore, each additional worker adds less output than the previous worker.

bullets.text: Short run: Law of Variable Proportions ⇒ Variation in Marginal product of labour (MPL)

Law of Variable Proportions: As successive units of a variable input are added to a fixed input, the marginal product of the variable input first increases, reaches a maximum, and eventually decreases.

Initially, the fixed input is underutilised. Adding variable inputs allows: Specialisation (workers can divide tasks), better coordination (workers can assist each other) and better utilisation of the fixed input (machines/factory space are used more effectively).
So each additional worker can contribute more than the previous worker.

Eventually, the fixed input becomes a constraint. Too many variable inputs sharing the same machines means workers have to wait for machines, the space becomes crowded and opportunities for further specialisation are already exhausted.

slides.title: Guiding the Production Process
slides.text:
Guiding the Production Process
Producing on the production function
Aligning incentives to induce maximum worker effort.
Employing the right level of inputs
When labor or capital vary in the short run, to maximize profit a manager will hire
labor until the value of marginal product of labor equals the wage: VMPL = w, where VMPL = P x MPL.
capital until the value of marginal product of capital equals the rental rate: VMPK = r, where VMPK = P x MPK .

slides.title: Question

Question
A firm's total cost function is: TC = 100 + 20Q + 2Q2.
Find:
Fixed cost
Variable cost
Average total cost
Average variable cost
Marginal cost
ATC when Q = 10
MC when Q = 10

bullets.text: A firm's total cost function is: TC = 100 + 20Q + 2Q2.

slides.title: Solution:
slides.text:
Solution:
TC = 100 + 20Q + 2Q2
1. Fixed cost
The constant term is 100. Therefore, FC = 100
2. Variable cost
VC = 20Q + 2Q2
3. Average total cost
ATC = TC / Q
ATC = (100/Q) +20+2Q
4. Average variable cost
AVC = TVC/Q = 20+2Q
5. Marginal cost
MC = dTC/dQ (differentiate TC w.r.t. Q)
MC = 20+4Q
6. ATC when Q = 10
ATC= (100/Q) +20+2Q = (100/10) + 20 + 2*10 = 50
7. MC when Q = 10
MC = 20+4Q = 20 + 4*10 = 60

bullets.text: The constant term is 100. Therefore, FC = 100

slides.title: Economies of Scale and the U-Shaped LRAC Curve
slides.text:
Economies of Scale and the U-Shaped LRAC Curve
Economies of Scale ⇒ Falling LRAC
As output increases: Q↑ ⇒ LRAC↓
Why?
Greater specialisation and division of labour
Better utilisation of machinery and other resources
Bulk purchasing and input discounts
Spreading fixed/setup costs over more units
Greater scope for managerial and technical efficiencies
Diseconomies of Scale ⇒ Rising LRAC
Beyond an optimal scale: Q↑ ⇒ LRAC↑
Why?
Managerial and coordination difficulties
Bureaucracy and slower decision-making
Difficulty monitoring a very large organisation
Congestion and organisational complexity

slides.title: Economies of Scope
slides.text:
Economies of Scope
C(Q1, 0) + C(0, Q2) > C(Q1, Q2).
It is cheaper to produce the two outputs jointly instead of separately.
Example:
It is cheaper for Time-Warner to produce Internet connections and Instant Messaging services jointly than separately.
